planting.note: Set out bare-root or containerized saplings in early spring once the ground has thawed and workable, mulching well to retain moisture around the developing taproot; seed requires 30-60 days cold-moist stratification.

directions: Set out bare-root or containerized saplings in early spring once the ground has thawed and workable, mulching well to retain moisture around the developing taproot. This fast-growing oak establishes a broad, rounded canopy that turns deep russet-red in autumn and casts dense summer shade over patios and large lawns. Its acorns mature in two seasons and feed deer, turkey, and squirrels, making it a cornerstone wildlife tree for parks and naturalized landscapes. Avoid heavy pruning after establishment since red oaks are more susceptible to oak wilt when wounded during the growing season.

planting.note: Plant young trees in fall on well-drained, rocky or sandy slopes where this ridge-loving oak naturally thrives, since it tolerates drought and poor soil far better than bottomland oaks.

directions: Plant young trees in fall on well-drained, rocky or sandy slopes where this ridge-loving oak naturally thrives, since it tolerates drought and poor soil far better than bottomland oaks. Its thick, deeply furrowed bark and coarse, chestnut-like leaves give strong winter and textural interest in naturalized or restoration plantings. Because it resists rot and drought stress once established, it is an excellent long-lived specimen for dry hillsides, ridgetops, and low-maintenance shade areas. Acorns are relatively large, low in tannin, and readily eaten by wildlife.

planting.note: Transplant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early fall or early spring into deep, well-drained soil away from road salt and compacted urban sites, since sugar maple is sensitive to both.

directions: Transplant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early fall or early spring into deep, well-drained soil away from road salt and compacted urban sites, since sugar maple is sensitive to both. This long-lived tree develops a dense, rounded crown prized for the brilliant orange and scarlet fall color that defines much of the eastern hardwood forest, and mature stands are the traditional source of maple syrup sap. It provides excellent shade for large residential and park settings but needs consistent moisture during establishment and should be kept out of confined urban tree pits. Give it room to grow undisturbed for decades, as it is intolerant of heavy pruning and soil disturbance near its roots.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall into loamy, well-drained ground; more tolerant of floodplain soils and drought than sugar maple.

directions: Closely related to sugar maple but more tolerant of floodplain soils and drought, this tree should be planted from container stock in fall into loamy, well-drained ground. Its distinctive drooping, three-lobed leaves with fuzzy undersides and thick, fissured bark distinguish it from sugar maple, and it produces similarly vivid gold-to-orange fall foliage. It works well as a durable street or park shade tree in the upper Midwest and can also be tapped for syrup like its close relative. Once established it needs little supplemental care beyond occasional deep watering during extended dry spells.

planting.note: Plant in cool, moist, well-drained soil in early spring, ideally clustered in groups of three or more where the papery, exfoliating bark can be admired year-round.

directions: Plant in cool, moist, well-drained soil in early spring, ideally clustered in groups of three or more where the strikingly white, papery, exfoliating bark can be admired year-round against evergreens or dark backdrops. This fast-growing, relatively short-lived pioneer tree tolerates cold climates exceptionally well but struggles in prolonged heat and drought, so it performs best in northern gardens rather than the warmer end of its range. Its golden fall color and open canopy make it a favorite specimen for naturalized woodland edges, and the bark historically provided material for canoes and baskets. Keep roots consistently moist and mulched, since paper birch is prone to bronze birch borer when stressed by heat or drought.
